notes.author: Chloe Nakamura
notes.text: Kickoff with Frank Bellweather. Selecting a SaaS claims platform to replace a mainframe system. Irene Szabo insists the new platform replicate 140+ existing claims workflows exactly.

notes.author: Hugo Lambert
notes.text: Vendor selected. To meet Irene's requirement, 60% of the configuration budget went into custom code extensions rather than standard configuration.

notes.author: Hugo Lambert
notes.text: Vendor released a major platform upgrade; 34 of our custom extensions broke. Upgrade blocked. Remediation estimate $480k.

notes.author: Chloe Nakamura
notes.text: Frank ordered a workflow rationalization: 140 workflows reduced to 38 using vendor-standard patterns. Irene reluctantly agreed after adjusters said half the old workflows were workarounds for mainframe limits.

notes.author: Hugo Lambert
notes.text: Re-implemented on standard configuration. Upgrades now apply cleanly. Frank: "We paid twice for the same system."

simulation.lesson: When adopting a packaged or SaaS platform, heavily customizing it to replicate legacy workflows backfires: custom extensions break on vendor upgrades and the organization ends up paying twice. Rationalizing workflows to fit the platform's standard patterns first — many legacy steps turn out to be workarounds for old system limits — gives a sustainable result.
simulation.why: Custom code on a vendor platform accumulates upgrade debt; many legacy workflows only exist because of old system constraints.
simulation.conditions: Packaged/SaaS platform with frequent vendor releases, strong pressure to replicate legacy processes.
